output.text_response:
**All 18 assertions from the two census records have been linked to the right tree persons.** Here's a summary of what was done:

---

### 1860 Salt Lake County Census (src_001)
Four household members linked with **high confidence (match score 0.78)**:

| Record Person | Tree Person | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Joseph Pratt (head, ~b. 1822, England) | I1 | Zero-year birth gap |
| Ann Pratt (wife, ~b. 1825, England) | I2 | Zero-year birth gap |
| Sarah Pratt (daughter, ~b. 1847, England) | I3 | Zero-year birth gap |
| Joseph Pratt Jr. (son, ~b. 1850, England) | I4 | Zero-year birth gap |

---

### 1880 Salt Lake County Census (src_002)
Three household members linked with **high confidence**:

| Record Person | Tree Person | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Joseph Pratt (head, age 58, England) | I1 | Relationship assertions also linked |
| Ann Pratt (wife, age 55, England) | I2 | "Wife of" assertion linked |
| Joseph Pratt Jr. (son, age 30, England) | I4 | "Son of" assertion linked |

---

### Notable Observation
**Sarah Pratt is absent from the 1880 household** — she would have been ~33. She may have married (and been enumerated under a married name), died before 1880, or been living elsewhere. A natural next step would be to search for Sarah Pratt in marriage records or later censuses after 1860.

There were four minor advisory warnings on pre-existing non-geocoded place facts (I1–I4), all pre-existing and not introduced by this work.

Four `nonStandardPlace` advisory warnings on I1–I4 — all pre-existing, all on old Cranfield birth/residence facts that lacked geocoded standard places before this run. Advisory-level only; nothing contradicts identity or introduces an impossibility.

---

**What was linked and why**

All 18 assertions across the two census records were linked to the right people in the tree with high confidence. In the 1860 Salt Lake County census, the household head is Joseph Pratt, born in England around 1822 — his name, estimated birth year, birthplace, and position as the head of a household containing Ann Pratt (wife, born England ~1825), Sarah Pratt (daughter, born England ~1847), and Joseph Pratt (son, born England ~1850) all match the tree family exactly, down to zero years' gap on every birth estimate. The match score from FamilySearch's comparison tool was 0.78 for all four family members, which falls in the strong range. The family moved from Cranfield, Bedfordshire, England to Salt Lake County, Utah — roughly 7,767 km — but the FamilySearch wiki on Utah immigration notes that "many Latter-day Saint immigrants leaving Europe and Great Britain came on chartered ships from Liverpool, England," naming that corridor directly, which accounts for the move. All four 1860 household members are linked very confidently to the matching tree people.

The 1880 Salt Lake County census shows the same household — Joseph (head, now age 58, born England), Ann (wife, age 55, born England), and Joseph Jr (son, age 30, born England) — again matching I1, I2, and I4 with zero-year birth gaps and the same corridor. The 1880 record adds explicit "wife of" and "son of" relationship statements that were linked to both parties named. One family member is absent from 1880: Sarah Pratt would be about 33 by then. She may have married and been enumerated under a married name, died before the census, or been living elsewhere — this is a natural next question.

The next useful step would be to search for Sarah Pratt after 1860 to find out what happened to her — a marriage record or a later census under a different surname would resolve her absence from the 1880 household.

The children are marked as **probable** rather than certain because they appear in this one record only and no independent source yet confirms them. quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

The 1913 San Francisco marriage record of Amelie Ottilie Gaetjen to William Chadwick Fralich names Hermann Gaetjen as the bride's father and Amelia Nichols as her mother. All three people have been confidently matched to the right tree members:

- **Hermann Gaetjen (I1)** — father of the bride, similarity score **0.97**. The record also names his wife as Amelia Nichols, which rules out both namesakes on file: one was born in 1873 (only five years old when Hermann's son Henry was born in 1878) and the other lived in Butte County and died in 1899.
- **Amelia Nichols (I4)** — mother of the bride, similarity score **0.96**.
- **Amelie Ottilie Gaetjen (I3)** — the bride, similarity score **0.95**; the one-year birth-year difference (1883 vs. 1884) falls within normal self-reporting variation.

**What was updated in the tree:**
- I3 gained a name-spelling variant (*Amelie Ottilie Gaetjen*) and her birth fact was enriched with the new source reference.
- I1 and I4 each gained a source reference on their existing names.

**Pre-existing note:** I3 carries a 1935 Residence fact with the value "Same House" and no standard place; this predates this session and was not introduced by the records linked here.

**Next step:** Link the remaining assertions from src_001 and src_002 to build out evidence toward answering the main question — when and from where in Germany Hermann Gaetjen immigrated.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

Links created: pe_001–pe_011. Materialization result: I3 gained one name spelling (Amelie Ottilie Gaetjen) and had her birth fact enriched with the new source ref; I1 and I4 each gained one source reference on their existing names.

One pre-existing warning on I3: her 1935 Residence fact carries the value "Same House" with no standard place. This predates this linking session (sourced only to the FamilySearch Family Tree baseline read) and was not introduced by any record linked here.

---

The 1913 San Francisco marriage record of Amelie Ottilie Gaetjen to William Chadwick Fralich names Hermann Gaetjen as the bride's father and Amelia Nichols as her mother. All three people have been confidently matched to the right members of the family. The match for Hermann as the father is very strong (similarity score 0.97): the name matches exactly, and the record also names his wife as Amelia Nichols, which is the detail that rules out the two other Hermann Gaetjens on file — one of those was only five years old when Hermann's son Henry was born, and the other lived in a different county and died in 1899. The match for Amelia Nichols as the mother (score 0.96) and for the bride Amelie Ottilie as the daughter already in the family tree (score 0.95, with a one-year birth-year difference that falls well within normal self-reporting variation) are equally confident. The marriage record adds the bride's name spelling as a variant on her tree entry and attaches itself as a source to all three family members.

The next step is to link the remaining assertions from the other two records (src_001 and src_002) to the right people, which will build out the evidence toward answering the main question about when and from where in Germany Hermann Gaetjen immigrated.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments

The tree_query retrieved the correct persons (I1, I3, I4). The same_person calls correctly scored each assertion against its tree person, with proper recordRole parameters supplied for relationship assertions (a_025, a_026, a_027) where the second party differed from the assertion's own party. The materialize_facts call correctly specified the three persons and their record roles. The person_warnings call checked all three persons for conflicts.

dimensions.name: Confidence calibration
dimensions.rationale: All confidence levels are correctly calibrated to the evidence strength. Hermann Gaetjen (a_020, a_027, a_025 to I1) is marked confident with score 0.97 because: (1) the record names his wife Amelia Nichols (I4), uniquely identifying him among the two namesakes; (2) one namesake was born 1873 (too young to father Henry b. 1878); (3) the other was born 1827 and died 1899 in Butte County with no connection to Amelia Nichols. Amelia Nichols (a_021, a_026, a_027 to I4) is confident with score 0.96: name matches exactly, husband Hermann Gaetjen confirmed in same record, no competing candidates. The bride (a_022-a_026 to I3) is confident with score 0.95: one-year birth discrepancy (1884 vs 23 Aug 1883) falls within normal self-reporting variation on marriage certificates; parents Hermann and Amelia Nichols confirmed; residence consistent (San Francisco 1913 vs 1920). All confidence tiers match the identity-evidence strength.

For I1: name matches exactly, score 0.97, namesake cap met by noting the two other Hermann Gaetjens cannot be this father (one too young, one died 1899 in different county), and crucially, the record names his wife Amelia Nichols uniquely identifying him. For I4: name matches exactly, score 0.96, husband Hermann Gaetjen confirmed, no competing candidates. For I3: birth year discrepancy explained (1 year within normal variation), residence consistent (San Francisco 1913 marriage vs 1920 residence), name is spelling variant, parents Hermann and Amelia Nichols match tree parents exactly. Rationales explain why competing candidates were ruled out and cite the specific evidence tying each person to the record.
